summary: While Britain fought Napoleon, its blockade of France and the impressment of seamen from American ships angered the United States, and Americans blamed Britain for backing Indigenous resistance in the Old Northwest, where the Shawnee leader Tecumseh had built a confederacy of nations. Some Americans also hoped to annex Canada. Congress declared war in June 1812, but invasions of Upper and Lower Canada failed, and in August 1812 an American army surrendered Detroit to British troops and Tecumseh's warriors. In 1813 Oliver Hazard Perry won control of Lake Erie and Tecumseh was killed at the Thames, while in the south the Creek War ended in 1814 with heavy Creek land cessions. After Napoleon's defeat in 1814 Britain went on the offensive, burning Washington, but it was repulsed at Baltimore and Plattsburgh. The Treaty of Ghent, signed in December 1814, restored the prewar borders. Andrew Jackson's victory at New Orleans came weeks later, before news of the peace arrived. Canada stayed British, while Indigenous nations lost most of their remaining lands south of the Great Lakes.
casualties: An estimated 15,000 Americans died from all causes, about 2,200 of them in battle; British and Canadian deaths are estimated at up to about 10,000, and Indigenous nations lost an estimated 10,000 warriors and civilians, many from disease.

sources.title: Office of the Historian: The War of 1812, 1812–1815

brief.hook: Angered by British seizures of its ships and sailors, and by British backing for Indigenous resistance in the West, the United States declared war in 1812.

sides.who: The United States, with its small regular army, state militias, navy and privateers, and some Indigenous allies such as Cherokee and Choctaw warriors
Britain and its colonies of Upper and Lower Canada and the Maritimes, with Canadian militia and Indigenous nations of Tecumseh's confederacy

brief.resultLine: The Treaty of Ghent, signed on 24 December 1814 and ratified by the US Senate on 17 February 1815, restored the borders as they had been before the war.

strategies.name: Brock and Tecumseh's bluff
strategies.text: At Detroit in August 1812, Tecumseh's warriors circled through the woods to look far more numerous, and Brock warned of a massacre. General Hull surrendered over 2,000 men to a smaller force.

strategies.name: Command of the lakes
strategies.text: No army could invade without the Great Lakes. Perry's win on Lake Erie in 1813 let the Americans retake Detroit, and Macdonough's on Lake Champlain in 1814 sent a British invasion back to Canada.

strategies.name: The Royal Navy blockade
strategies.text: An ever tighter British blockade shut in American shipping, and once Napoleon fell, British troops raided the coast at will, burning Washington in 1814. Yet neither side could win a decisive victory.

impact: Canada stayed British, and Canadians came to remember the war as a successful defence against American invasion.
Tecumseh's death broke his confederacy, and Britain dropped its plan for a protected Indigenous homeland south of the Great Lakes.
In August 1814 Andrew Jackson forced the defeated Creeks to give up about 23 million acres of land.
Jackson's victory at New Orleans made him a national hero and gave Americans a triumphant memory of the war.

details: British orders in council restricting neutral trade with France, the impressment of seamen from American ships and British support for Indigenous resistance in the Northwest had soured relations for years. On 1 June President James Madison asked Congress for war. The House voted 79 to 49 and the Senate 19 to 13, and Madison signed the declaration on 18 June. Opposition was strongest among Federalists in New England, whose trade depended on peace with Britain.

On Brock's orders, Captain Charles Roberts set out from Fort St. Joseph with British soldiers, fur traders and voyageurs and Ojibwe, Odawa, Menominee, Ho-Chunk and Sioux warriors. They landed on Mackinac Island and hauled a cannon onto the heights above the fort. Its commander, who had not yet heard that war had been declared, surrendered on 17 July. The easy success drew more Indigenous nations to the British side.

General William Hull invaded Upper Canada from Detroit on 12 July, but with his supply line threatened by Tecumseh's warriors he retreated to Detroit. Isaac Brock crossed the river with British troops, Canadian militia and Tecumseh's fighters and warned that his Indigenous allies might be beyond his control in an assault. Hull surrendered on 16 August with more than 2,000 men. The defeat left the British in control of Michigan Territory for more than a year.

About 400 miles south-east of Halifax, the American frigate Constitution under Isaac Hull met the British frigate Guerriere under James Dacres. In a short, close action Guerriere's masts were shot away, and she was so badly damaged that her captors set her on fire. The British lost 15 killed and 78 wounded, the Americans 7 killed. Though of little military weight for the Royal Navy, the victory lifted American spirits days after Detroit fell.

American troops under Stephen Van Rensselaer crossed the Niagara River and seized the heights above Queenston. Brock was killed leading a counterattack early in the fighting. Roger Sheaffe then brought up British regulars, militia and Mohawk warriors under John Norton, while many New York militiamen refused to cross the river to reinforce their comrades. The Americans on the heights, among them Winfield Scott, surrendered; about 955 were taken prisoner.

An American force under James Winchester, advancing towards Detroit in midwinter, occupied Frenchtown on the River Raisin. On 22 January British troops and Indigenous warriors under Henry Procter attacked and forced it to surrender. Wounded American prisoners left behind were killed the next day, about 60 by some accounts. The killings became a rallying cry in Kentucky and the West and hardened American resolve to retake Detroit.

Using their new squadron on Lake Ontario, American forces landed near York and drove off the outnumbered British regulars, who blew up their powder magazine as they withdrew, killing and wounding many attackers, among them General Zebulon Pike. During an occupation of nearly two weeks American troops burned the legislative buildings and other public property. The raid gained little militarily, but the British later cited it when they burned Washington in 1814.

After a two-day bombardment, American troops stormed ashore at the mouth of the Niagara River on 27 May and captured Fort George. The retreating British struck back: a night attack at Stoney Creek on 5 June drove the American advance back, and on 24 June an American column surrendered at Beaver Dams to a smaller British and Indigenous force. The Americans were left holding little beyond Fort George itself.

In summer 1813 a civil war split the Creek Nation between the Red Sticks, who opposed land cessions and American ways, and Creeks who favoured accommodation. After American militia ambushed a Red Stick supply train at Burnt Corn in July, Red Stick warriors under Peter McQueen and William Weatherford stormed Fort Mims, a stockade about 35 miles north of Mobile, on 30 August. Most of the 500 or so militia, settlers and mixed-race Creek families inside were killed, and the Creek civil war became a war with the United States.

Both sides raced to build warships on Lake Erie. Near Put-in-Bay, Oliver Hazard Perry's squadron engaged Robert Barclay's. When Perry's flagship Lawrence was battered into surrender he crossed in a small boat to the Niagara and led a renewed attack, and all six British vessels struck their colours. 'We have met the enemy and they are ours,' Perry reported. Control of the lake cut the supply line of the British army at Detroit.

Without supplies by water, Henry Procter abandoned Detroit and Amherstburg and retreated up the Thames River, against Tecumseh's protests. William Henry Harrison's army of some 3,000 caught his roughly 950 British troops and Indigenous warriors near Moraviantown on 5 October. Richard Johnson's mounted infantry broke the British line, and Tecumseh was killed, after which his warriors withdrew. His death broke up the confederacy, and the United States regained Detroit and Michigan Territory.

In autumn 1813 two American armies advanced on Montreal. In late October Charles de Salaberry's small force of Canadian Voltigeurs, militia and Mohawk warriors turned back Wade Hampton's 4,000 men at the Châteauguay River. On 11 November, at Crysler's Farm on the St. Lawrence, about 800 British and Canadian troops under Joseph Morrison defeated James Wilkinson's rearguard of some 2,500. Both American armies withdrew into winter quarters, and Lower Canada was safe.

Abandoning Fort George in December, American militia burned the Canadian town of Newark on 10 December, leaving its people homeless in winter. The British retaliated across the Niagara frontier: they took Fort Niagara, raided and burned Lewiston, where civilians were killed, and on 30 December attacked and burned Buffalo and Black Rock. The cycle of reprisals left both banks of the Niagara devastated by the end of the year.

Andrew Jackson's Tennessee militia, US regulars and Cherokee and Creek allies attacked about 1,000 Red Sticks fortified in a bend of the Tallapoosa River. Some 800 Red Sticks were killed, against 49 of Jackson's men killed and 154 wounded. In the Treaty of Fort Jackson that August, Jackson forced the Creek Nation, including the Creeks who had fought beside him, to give up about 23 million acres, roughly half its land.

The Royal Navy had declared Chesapeake and Delaware Bays under blockade in December 1812. With Napoleon defeated and abdicated in April 1814, Britain sent more ships and veteran troops across the Atlantic, and on 31 May it extended the blockade to the entire coast. American exports, worth $130 million in 1807, fell to about $7 million in 1814, and customs revenue, the government's main income, fell by more than half.

Jacob Brown's American army crossed the Niagara River, took Fort Erie on 3 July and defeated a British force at Chippawa on 5 July. On 25 July it met the British again at Lundy's Lane, close to Niagara Falls, in a battle that raged into the night and became the costliest of the war. Neither side could claim victory, but the Americans fell back to Fort Erie, where they beat off a British assault in August.

A British force of about 4,500 under Robert Ross, guided by Rear Admiral George Cockburn, landed in Maryland and routed American militia at Bladensburg on 24 August. That evening the troops entered Washington and set fire to the Capitol, with the Library of Congress inside it, the President's House, the Treasury and the War Department. President Madison fled. The British, citing the burning of York, left after about a day.

Britain hoped to gain a land route between Halifax and Quebec in any peace. Its forces took Moose Island at Eastport in July, and in September John Sherbrooke led some 3,000 troops from Halifax up the Penobscot River, capturing Castine and destroying or seizing 17 American ships in a campaign of 26 days. The coast of Maine east of the Penobscot was held for the rest of the war and returned under the peace treaty.

George Prevost marched south from Canada along Lake Champlain with more than 8,000 troops. On 11 September Thomas Macdonough's American squadron, anchored in Plattsburgh Bay, defeated and captured the British flotilla, whose commander George Downie was killed. Without control of the lake to supply his army, Prevost called off the land attack and withdrew, weakening Britain's hand at the peace talks.

About 5,000 British troops landed at North Point to attack Baltimore. On 12 September American militia delayed them, and Robert Ross was killed by a sharpshooter. On 13 and 14 September British ships bombarded Fort McHenry for about 25 hours, but its garrison held, and the British withdrew. Seeing the flag still flying at dawn, the lawyer Francis Scott Key wrote the verses that became 'The Star-Spangled Banner'.

Peace talks had begun at Ghent in August 1814, with Britain at first demanding territory and an Indigenous buffer state. The British failures at Plattsburgh and Baltimore removed the case for territorial gains, and both sides settled for the prewar status quo. Signed on 24 December, the treaty returned captured territory, set up commissions for disputed boundaries and promised to restore Indigenous nations' rights of 1811, but it said nothing about impressment or neutral rights.

A British expedition under Edward Pakenham landed below New Orleans in December. On 8 January about 8,000 British troops assaulted Andrew Jackson's earthworks at Chalmette, defended by some 5,700 regulars, militia and volunteers. The attack failed within hours: the British lost about 2,000 killed, wounded or captured, Pakenham among the dead, while the Americans lost 71. The battle came after the treaty was signed but before word reached America.

News of the treaty reached Washington in February, just after news of New Orleans and as Federalist delegates from the Hartford Convention arrived with New England's complaints about the war. The Senate approved the treaty on 16 February and ratifications were exchanged on 17 February, ending the war. On the Gulf Coast the British had taken Fort Bowyer on 12 February, but word of peace halted their attack on Mobile.
